title: Wipe away tears (Isaiah 25:6–8)
hook: a feast of rich food for all peoples, and death swallowed up

segments.voice: Yesterday, Malachi's last promise, Elijah sent to turn the hearts of parents and children. Did you make the call or send the message? Day four hundred ninety-seven.

After a funeral, there's usually food. A long table in a church hall, casseroles under foil, someone's famous potato salad, coffee in big urns. People who haven't seen each other in years stand around holding paper plates, and between the tears there's sometimes laughter. Grief and a meal, side by side. Today the book of Isaiah takes that same table and turns it inside out: a feast where the guest list is everyone on earth. And the main thing that's been swallowed up, at the end of the meal, is death.
screen: `GRIEF AND A MEAL, SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the menu, in the King James Bible: "a feast of fat things, a feast of wines on the lees, of fat things full of marrow, of wines on the lees well refined." Fat things meant the best food, the richest cuts. Wine on the lees is wine left to age on its sediment until it's deep and smooth. This isn't a snack. It's a banquet, set on God's mountain, and it's for all people, every nation. Then the feast takes a turn. God removes the covering cast over all peoples, the veil spread over all nations. Some readers hear that as a burial shroud, the cloth laid over the dead, and it's lifted off the whole human race. And then this: "He will swallow up death in victory; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces." Some readers hear an echo of older stories from that region, where death was a swallower with a huge mouth. Here, the swallower gets swallowed. And then a gentle picture. After the victory, God doesn't make a speech. God goes face to face, wiping tears off cheeks, one by one, like a parent after a nightmare. The New Testament picks these words up twice. Paul quotes the swallowing of death when he writes about the resurrection. And near the very end of the Bible, Revelation says: "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes." Christians hear in this feast a picture of what they hope for. This week's prophets have walked us there: Habakkuk's yet, the God who sings, consider your ways, not by might, the donkey king, hearts turned. And now, a table set for everyone.
screen: then, large: `HE WILL SWALLOW UP DEATH IN VICTORY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share a good meal. Settle, and breathe. First, remember. Bring to mind someone you've lost, or someone grieving now. Let yourself feel it for a moment; Isaiah's feast doesn't skip the tears. Then picture a table. Who would you want at it? Someone lonely, someone far from home, someone you haven't eaten with in too long, someone who needs good food this week. Picture setting the plate in front of them. Then choose one real meal you can share: a dinner, a coffee, a dish dropped at a door. If you pray, you can give thanks for the people at your table. If you don't, simply plan the meal. The bell holds the time.
Wipe away tears. Isaiah's feast on God's mountain for all peoples, where death is swallowed up and God wipes the tears from every face.
Your line: tears wiped away. Today, share food with someone, and if they're carrying something heavy, let the meal be slow. Day four hundred ninety-seven, and another week on the path.

howItsDone: Isaiah 25:6–9 is among the funeral readings in some churches, and some Christians connect its feast with the communion meal and with the hope of resurrection.

options: wipe the tears from every face.
fork.reveal: "the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces." the victory ends in a close, personal gesture.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice line for a sympathy card.
what it means: Isaiah pictures a feast for all peoples on God's mountain, where the shroud is lifted, death is swallowed and every tear is wiped.
what a scholar hears: some readers hear the region's old stories of death as a swallower, so here the swallower is swallowed. Paul and Revelation both pick this up.

notes: Revelation 21:4 KJV reads 'And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes;' — quoted to the semicolon. Revelation 7:17 has a similar line.
The covering/veil of 25:7 as a burial shroud is a common interpretation, presented as 'many readers hear'.
Death as a swallowing figure: Canaanite/Ugaritic Mot is described with an enormous swallowing mouth. Stated generally as 'the old stories of that region'. Confirm.
'Wine on the lees' as wine aged on its sediment. Confirm.
